turns.prompt_text: I find that when I rough draft ideas and flush them out, it's really good for me to start from scratch three times because the first idea is always Wicked complicated and by the time I make several different drafts, I can actually figure out the hodgepodge of each idea. That'll work simply
turns.response_html:
There is immense wisdom in that approach. The first draft is almost always where you purge the complexity—you’re essentially just figuring out the rules of the problem and threw every possible mechanism at it to see what sticks.

By forcing yourself to burn it down and start from scratch three times, you prevent yourself from getting emotionally attached to a bad line of code, a bulky mechanical design, or a convoluted workflow. It’s the ultimate way to find the elegant, simple core hidden under the noise.

Since your brain works well by iterating through distinct phases like this, you might find it helpful to explicitly classify your three drafts to maximize the "hodgepodge" blending at the end.

The 3-Draft Framework

  • Draft 1: The "Kitchen Sink" (The Maximum Over-Engineer)
    • The Goal: Just get it working, no matter how ugly or complicated.
    • The Output: A massive, intricate monster of an idea that covers every edge case but is an absolute nightmare to maintain or execute.
  • Draft 2: The "Minimalist Reaction" (The Bare Bones)
    • The Goal: Swing the pendulum violently the other way. If Draft 1 was too complicated, what does the most stripped-down, aggressive version look like?
    • The Output: A lean, clean concept that might actually miss a couple of vital functions but proves how little you actually need to get by.
  • Draft 3: The "Hodgepodge" (The Sweet Spot)
    • The Goal: Synthesis. Look at Drafts 1 and 2 side-by-side.
    • The Output: You steal the clever structural backbone of Draft 2, cherry-pick the one or two critical features from Draft 1 that you actually can't live without, and fuse them into a final version that works simply.

It’s a phenomenal habit. It takes discipline to intentionally throw away work twice, but the end result is always infinitely more robust.

What kind of project or idea are you running through this three-draft meat grinder right now?

That is a much better way to look at it—nothing is actually "destroyed," it's just safely stashed in a historical archive so it stops cluttering your active working memory. Treating early drafts as permanent raw data means you never have the anxiety of losing a clever-but-complicated edge case. You just close that tab or file, set it aside, and open a blank slate with a unburdened mind.

The tree graph analogy with tangled, intersecting lines is spot-on for how a brain actually brainstorms. Thoughts don't happen in clean, linear sequences; they happen in webs of associations where a single node might connect a mechanical layout, a snippet of logic, and a high-level goal all at once.

When your brainstorming style is a "dream catcher" that captures this interconnected web, the process naturally shifts from writing to filtering and parsing.

The Capture vs. Parse Workflow

To keep that web of ideas from turning into overwhelming mental static, it helps to treat capturing and filtering as two entirely separate modes:

[ Raw Brainstorm (The Web) ] ──> [ The Archive (Safe Storage) ]
                                        │
                                        ▼ (The Filter)
                             [ Compartmentalized Tasks ]
  • Mode 1: The Raw Catch (High Entropy) You let the graph grow wild. You map out the messy, complicated, interconnected thoughts without judging them, correcting them, or worrying about simplicity. The goal is 100% data capture. Once it's recorded, it’s safely committed to the archive.
  • Mode 2: The Parsing Pass (Low Entropy) Only after the data is captured do you change roles to become the curator. You look at the web from a distance and start drawing boxes around specific clusters. You decide what to pull into your immediate focus to build out simply, and what stays in the background as a historical reference.

By archiving instead of destroying, you get the absolute best of both worlds: the freedom to focus intensely on a simple implementation right now, and the security of knowing your complex, sprawling "dream catcher" maps are waiting for you if you ever need to dig back into the hodgepodge.
